items.prompt: Which ask is most likely to get Maya a concrete answer?
choices: Could you take a look and give any feedback?
How's the pricing slide specifically?
Let me know if anything stands out.
items.explanation: A named slide gives the reviewer a concrete target, while the open asks let a polite reply do.

items.prompt: Why does "any feedback?" usually get "looks great!"?
choices: People never have real opinions on others' work
Coworkers are rarely allowed to criticize a draft
A vague reply is the cheapest one to give
items.explanation: A vague reply takes no effort and carries no risk, so it is what most people give.

items.prompt: What does narrowing a feedback question change?
choices: It makes a generic answer hard to give
It makes the reviewer read much more slowly
It makes the reviewer like you
items.explanation: A narrow question makes a vague reply look like skipping the named part, so a real one comes.

items.prompt: Did Jordan's honesty change between ask 1 and ask 2?
choices: Yes, Jordan became more honest
No, only the question's scope and shape changed
Yes, Jordan had hidden things
items.explanation: Jordan's opinion stayed the same. The scope of the question changed what could be extracted.

items.prompt: Which scope is easier to answer from a real memory?
choices: How did Tuesday's call go?
How am I doing overall, in general?
How would you describe my work lately?
items.explanation: One recent event can be recalled, while an overall impression has to be improvised.

items.prompt: A reviewer says "looks good" to a vague ask. What is the best reading?
choices: The work was flawless, so nothing is left to say
The work was poor
It tells you little either way
items.explanation: A vague reply to a vague ask would come whether or not concerns exist, so it says little.

items.prompt: Narrow questions mainly help because they...
choices: Ask the reviewer to hurry
Let the asker avoid criticism
Give the reviewer something concrete to look at
items.explanation: A concrete target is what lets a reviewer give a concrete answer instead of a polite default.

items.prompt: What is the trap of waiting for a yearly review to ask for feedback?
choices: Reviews are always negative
Months of repeating a fixable mistake
Nobody is allowed to comment in between those reviews
items.explanation: Waiting for a scheduled review leaves long stretches where nobody asked a specific question.

items.prompt: Dan wrote an onboarding checklist yesterday and wants real feedback. Which ask fits this unit best?
choices: Could you give it a look and tell me what you think of the whole thing?
I'd love any thoughts when you have a spare moment sometime this week.
Could you check step 4, the account setup? I'm unsure the order is right.
Is it good? I'm hoping it's ready to share with everyone by today.
items.explanation: Step 4 is one specific, checkable part, so a vague reply no longer fits. The other asks leave the target open or invite a quick yes.
items.reference:
Same person, three question shapes
🤷 "any feedback?" → "looks great!"
🎯 "how's the pricing slide?" → a real gap
🔍 "did you read it all?" → known coverage
Why: a vague question makes a vague reply the cheapest one, and a narrow question removes that exit.
items.learnMore:
The question decides the answer

Jordan's opinion was the same in all three asks. What changed was how much effort and risk each question attached to a real answer versus a polite one.

Common mistake

Concluding that a coworker has nothing to say because a vague ask got a vague reply.
items.reflection: Think of the last time you asked "any thoughts?" about something you made. What narrower question could you have asked instead?

items.prompt: Nina asks "how does the opening paragraph read?" and hears "looks fine." Sam asks "any thoughts?" and hears "looks fine." Which reply says more about the work?
choices: Nina's, since a lazy reply to a named part is costlier
Sam's, since an open question gives much more room for the reviewer to raise concerns
Neither, since identical words always carry identical information whoever asks them
Sam's, since shorter questions tend to get more candid answers from busy people
items.explanation: It is still only a clue. But a vague reply to a named part reads as not having looked, so it is a bit likelier to reflect a real look.

choices: The worry is right, so the widest possible question is always the safest choice for an asker
The worry is right, so narrow asks should be avoided whenever the work is important
The worry is wrong, since reviewers only ever read the parts they were asked about
Narrowing makes a concrete reply possible, and coverage can be checked later
items.explanation: Narrowing does not forbid other comments, it just makes a concrete one possible. The coverage follow-up exists to learn about the unasked parts.

choices: A lot, since stating urgency forces a detailed reply from any reviewer
Little, since it does not narrow the target and a vague reply stays cheapest
A lot, since effort is driven by how much the asker cares
Nothing, since reviewers ignore the wording of every request
items.explanation: Shape matters more than how much the asker needs the answer. Urgency adds pressure but leaves the easy vague exit open.

items.prompt: What is calibration?
choices: Deciding whether the reviewer is lying
Deciding which reviewer to ask next, and when
Deciding how much weight an answer deserves
items.explanation: Calibration is weighting an answer by how much work stands behind it.

items.prompt: Two people both say "looks good", but one read every line and one skimmed. What differs?
choices: The worth of the same words
Whether the words are honest in this case
Whether the deck is good or bad overall
items.explanation: The words are identical, but they carry different information depending on what was read.

items.prompt: Which follow-up helps you calibrate?
choices: Are you sure you really meant what you said?
Did you read all of it, or just that part?
Why not say it sooner?
items.explanation: A coverage question reveals how much of the work the answer is based on.

items.prompt: Is calibration about not believing people?
choices: No, it weighs an answer by how much work stands behind it
Yes, doubt each answer
Yes, for praise only
items.explanation: Calibration scales trust. It does not mean doubting people by default.

items.prompt: What does "mainly the pricing slide" tell Maya?
choices: That Jordan dislikes the rest of the deck
That the pricing slide is perfect and needs no changes
How much of the deck was reviewed
items.explanation: It sets a boundary: the pricing slide was read and the rest was not read closely.

items.prompt: Calibration asks you to consider...
choices: How long they have worked at the company and in which team
How friendly they sounded
How much of the work they actually saw
items.explanation: How much the person saw, and what they have caught before, shape how much the reply is worth.

items.prompt: A fast, generic answer is best treated as...
choices: Proof that nothing was read
A clue worth one specific follow-up
Proof that everything was read
items.explanation: A fast generic reply is a clue, not a verdict, so one specific question is the right response.

items.prompt: When is a follow-up question worth asking?
choices: Only when the answer is critical
When the answer is too smooth to show coverage
Never, because a second question is always rude to ask
items.explanation: When the answer cannot show what was reviewed, a follow-up supplies the missing information.

items.prompt: Leo gets two replies to his proposal within the hour. Ana: "solid, I liked the budget table." Raj: "solid." Which is best calibrated?
choices: Both deserve equal weight, since both used the word solid and both came quickly
Raj's deserves more weight, since a shorter reply is more likely to be honest
Neither deserves any weight, since fast replies are always careless and incomplete
Ana's detail is checkable, so weigh it more; ask Raj a follow-up
items.explanation: A detail Leo can check is a clue of engagement. The bare reply is not worthless, but one question about what Raj read tells Leo how far to lean on it.
items.reference:
Same words, different weight
📖 reviewer A read every line: "looks good" is strong
👀 reviewer B skimmed: "looks good" is weak
❓ one follow-up tells you which you got
Why: calibration means weighting an answer by how much work stands behind it.
items.learnMore:
Weighing, not doubting

Calibration asks how much of the work the person saw and what they have caught before. It adjusts how strongly you rely on an answer. It does not mean assuming people are wrong.

Common mistake

Treating calibration as suspicion, and so arguing with reviewers instead of asking about coverage.
items.reflection: Pick a piece of feedback you received recently. Do you know how much of your work the person actually looked at?

items.prompt: After a reviewer says "the rest looks fine", which response treats calibration correctly?
choices: Ignore it, since praise cannot be trusted
Ask which sections they read, then trust the answer in proportion
Accept it fully, since they would have said otherwise
Ask them to repeat it more firmly in writing
items.explanation: Calibration scales trust to the work behind the answer. It is neither blanket acceptance nor blanket doubt.

Skip any follow-up, since a strong record settles coverage

Treat it like any reply, since a track record is irrelevant
items.explanation: A record raises the starting trust, but it does not tell you which parts of this particular work were read.

choices: It was the cheapest reply available
The work is flawless in every respect
The reviewer is lying to you
items.explanation: It is the cheapest reply whether or not concerns exist, so it tells you little about the work.

items.prompt: What does a narrow question remove?
choices: The reviewer's honesty and willingness to say it
The easy vague exit
The need to read the work
items.explanation: Narrowing the question takes away the easy way to answer without engaging.

items.prompt: Why can "looks good" to "how's the pricing slide?" feel costly?
choices: It reads as not having looked at the slide
It breaks a company rule about how reviews are done
It always gets challenged
items.explanation: Answering a named target with a bare "looks good" suggests the target was not examined.

items.prompt: If a vague ask gets only "looks great", what does the missing detail tell you about?
choices: The work more than the question
The reviewer's mood that day
The question more than the work itself
items.explanation: The reply would arrive either way, so the lack of detail points at the question.

items.prompt: Is "looks good" necessarily a lie?
choices: Yes, it is always dishonest and deliberate
Yes, unless it comes in writing
No, it is a resting point
items.explanation: It is the natural resting point of a vague question and not necessarily dishonest.

items.prompt: What makes a vague answer easy to give?
choices: It requires reading the entire document
It takes no effort and has no social risk
It has to be defended in a meeting afterward
items.explanation: A vague reply needs no reading and exposes the reviewer to no risk, so it is easy.

items.prompt: After a narrow question, the easiest remaining answer is...
choices: A polite blank one
A real, specific one, the easiest left
No answer
items.explanation: Once the vague exit is closed, a real answer is the cheapest one left.

items.prompt: What does the vague reply depend on most?
choices: The work's quality, not the question's shape
Only how well you happen to know the reviewer
The question's shape, not the work's quality
items.explanation: The same work gets a different reply depending on how the question is shaped.

items.prompt: Sam asks a vague "what do you think?" about a draft, hears "seems fine!", and concludes it has no problems. What is the flaw?
choices: "Seems fine" is always sarcasm, so the reply really means the opposite of what was said
The reply is too short, and only long replies can ever be trusted as real feedback
The reply is the cheapest answer either way, so it is weak evidence
Sam should have waited a week, since reviewers become more honest as time passes
items.explanation: A reply that would be given regardless of the truth carries little information. Sam learned about the question, not the draft.
items.reference:
Where a vague question settles
🛋️ vague ask → cheapest reply is "looks good"
🚪 narrow ask → vague reply reads as not looking
🎯 a real answer becomes the cheaper one
Why: the effort and social risk attached to each possible reply decide which one people give.

items.prompt: Which signal suggests careful review?
choices: A friendly tone that makes the asker feel good
A specific reference to actual content
A very fast reply
items.explanation: Naming real content shows the person engaged with the work, which is why it earns weight.

items.prompt: A fast reply with generic language suggests...
choices: Possibly skimmed, so follow up
Definitely careful and complete work
Definitely dishonest, rushed, and careless
items.explanation: Speed and generic wording are clues of a skim, so a follow-up is worth asking before relying on it.

items.prompt: A track record of catching issues gives...
choices: A guarantee that they are right this time
Permission to skip all checks
Higher starting trust in that person
items.explanation: A record raises your starting trust, but it does not tell you the current reply is right.

items.prompt: Feedback that always repeats what you believed deserves...
choices: More trust than any other feedback gets
Immediate dismissal
A check on whether they agree by default
items.explanation: Constant agreement may mean shared judgment or habit, so it is worth checking.

items.prompt: Are the signals proof?
choices: Yes, any single one of them is proof
No, they are clues
Yes, but only the first two are
items.explanation: Each signal is a clue about engagement, not proof of it.

items.prompt: Can a fast answer still be careful?
choices: No, fast always means careless in practice
Yes, fast does not rule out careful
Only if it is also long
items.explanation: Speed alone does not decide quality, so treat it as one clue among several.

items.prompt: Can a specific answer be wrong?
choices: No, specific answers are always right
Only when spoken
Yes, specific is not the same as correct
items.explanation: Specific answers show engagement, but being specific does not make the content correct.

items.prompt: A manager's silence on a section can mean...
choices: Either no issues or not reached
Definitely no issues
Definitely disapproval of that section
items.explanation: Silence has two readings, and only a direct question tells them apart.

items.prompt: Mara gets P: "fine" in 2 minutes from someone who caught bugs in her docs before, and Q: "the retry section skips the timeout case" from a first-time reviewer. What is best?
choices: Take Q's checkable claim seriously and ask P which parts were read
Rely on P entirely, since a track record outweighs any specific claim
Dismiss Q, since a first-time reviewer has no record to weigh
Dismiss both, since neither came with proof
items.explanation: Q can be verified against the doc, and P's record raises trust without telling Mara what P covered.
items.reference:
Clues for weighting an answer
📌 names real content → weigh more
⚡ fast and generic → follow up first
📈 past catches → higher starting trust
🪞 always agrees → check independence
Why: each signal is a clue about engagement, and none of them is proof.
items.learnMore:

A fast answer can be careful and a specific answer can be wrong. The signals tell you where to ask a follow-up, not what the answer is worth.

Common mistake

Treating a single signal, such as speed, as a verdict on the whole reply.
items.reflection: Who in your week gives feedback you would weight most? Which signals make you trust them?

items.prompt: What is psychological safety?
choices: Feeling an honest answer will not be punished
Feeling sure that the work is already perfect and polished
Feeling liked
items.explanation: Safety is the expectation that candor will not bring punishment, mockery, or defensiveness.

items.prompt: A narrow question put to someone who fears criticism gets...
choices: A guaranteed candid answer
No answer at all, since silence is safest
Still a safe, vague answer
items.explanation: The question removes the excuse for vagueness but not the fear that keeps the reply safe.

items.prompt: What does a narrow question remove?
choices: The fear of an honest answer
The need for trust of any kind
The excuse for a vague answer
items.explanation: It closes the easy exit. It does not change whether the person feels safe being candid.

items.prompt: Which reaction builds safety?
choices: Arguing with the critique for ten minutes
Thanking them and using the useful part
Explaining at length why the critique is wrong
items.explanation: Thanking people and using their input shows that candor is welcome and worth the effort.

items.prompt: Is safety a step in the four-step procedure?
choices: Yes, it is the fourth step of the four
No, it sits under all four
Yes, it is the first step in the list
items.explanation: A good question and a calibration follow-up both depend on the person feeling safe.

items.prompt: Someone got an argument for honest criticism. Next time they may...
choices: Give even more detailed criticism
Ask to review less often and for fewer people
Choose the safe "looks fine"
items.explanation: People repeat what protected them. If candor cost an argument, they may avoid it again.

items.prompt: The two halves of the skill are...
choices: Better-shaped questions plus rewarding candor
Longer questions and faster replies
Formal reviews and written forms
items.explanation: The skill has two halves, and each fails without the other.

items.prompt: In the demo model, what does low safety do?
choices: Makes the question less narrow
Caps useful comments even for a narrow question
Raises the number of useful comments that get through
items.explanation: In the teaching model, safety scales how many of the possible useful comments get through.

items.prompt: Priya asks a perfectly narrow question of a coworker she snapped at last week for criticizing her slides. She hears "looks fine." Best explanation?
choices: Her question was too narrow, so widening it would fix the problem
Her question was fine, but the coworker may expect candor to cost them
The coworker has not read the slides, which proves a lack of effort
Coworkers never give candid replies to narrow questions, whoever asks them
items.explanation: Narrowing closes the easy exit. A coworker who expects an argument still has a reason to stay safe.
items.reference:
Safety caps question quality
🛡️ 100% safety: fully narrow ask yields 3.0 comments
🛡️ 60% safety: 2.0 comments
🛡️ 20% safety: 1.1 comments
Why: a narrow question removes the excuse for vagueness, not the fear of candor.
items.learnMore:
Two halves of one skill

Ask better-shaped questions, and make candor safe by thanking people for specific criticism, using the useful part, and saying what you changed. The numbers come from the unit's teaching model, not a measurement.

Common mistake

Perfecting the question while arguing with every critique you receive.
items.reflection: Think of someone who gives you honest feedback. What have you done in the past that made that easier for them?

items.prompt: In the teaching model, a fully narrow question yields 3.0 useful comments at 100% safety and 1.1 at 20%. What does that gap show?
choices: Narrow questions are worthless unless safety is already full
Safety matters little once the question is narrow enough
Low safety can cost more than half the value of a perfect question
Safety only changes how polite replies sound, not their count
items.explanation: 1.1 of 3.0 is about 37%, so roughly 63% is lost. It is a simplified model, but it makes the cap visible.

items.prompt: You want to raise safety over the next month. Which action fits the unit best?

Perfecting the question while arguing with every critique you receive.

A written review

What each reply contained

The unit counts checkable claims, such as a named gap, a named section, or a coverage statement. This is the unit's own definition, and it ignores word count on purpose.

items.prompt: Ben gets a specific comment on slide 3 and ships the deck, assuming the rest was checked. Which unit idea did he skip?

items.explanation: A specific answer about one part is silent on the rest. Asking what was read is what shows the gap.

Shorter

items.explanation: People repeat what proves useful, so visible action makes the next honest reply worthwhile.

Skipped
Narrow and specific too
items.explanation: Specific does not require finished, so a narrow early check works.

items.prompt: Which is an interrogation?
choices: How's the pricing slide specifically?
Don't you usually review more carefully?
Which sections did you read so far, please?
items.explanation: It asks about the reviewer's habits, not about the work or its coverage.

items.prompt: Jordan points out a gap and Maya says "thanks" but changes nothing. Weeks later a new ask gets "looks great." What does the unit suggest?
choices: Jordan lost the skill of reviewing, which fades without regular practice

Jordan is saving all the candid comments for the final review before the deadline
items.explanation: Acting visibly on feedback is what pays for the next honest answer. Without it, the cheap reply wins again.

Four ways the habit breaks
🕵️ interrogation: asking about the reviewer
🏁 only asking when finished: direction found late
📭 no visible action: answers stop coming
😤 defensive coverage question: reads as an audit
Why: each failure either raises the cost of an honest answer or hides what it could have told you.
